transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-04
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (SE), Mateo (CSM) — Samir (CTO), Lena (Platform), Mei (SRE), Rajiv (Security)

Summary: quick sync after Tuesday's eviction event where preprod experienced a memory eviction wave on edge nodes during an internal load test. Primary impact was elevated latency and a small percentage of truncated responses. Discussed root-cause hypotheses (KV cache under pressure, bad prefix caching, warmup behavior), mitigations (short term dedicated pool, fallback smoothing), and the runbook updates and benchmarks we will share.

Topics: incident timeline, repro plan, telemetry required, security/compliance questions (audit logs, KMS), pricing/contract impact, follow-up bench schedule

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I think we have about an hour. We'll do a light recap, then Priya will share what we repro'd on our end and the traces, and then we'll talk mitigations and next steps.
[00:23] Samir: Thanks Alex. Quick context — we ran a churny load test across our edge fleet yesterday, about 40% more sustained qps and short sessions. At 14:12 UTC we saw a sharp rise in token latencies and some 502-ish truncations. It recovered when we drained a couple of nodes but we saw another blip at 14:40, so it wasn't a one-off.
[01:05] Priya: Right, we saw the logs — on our side the pattern looked like a coordinated eviction wave. The KV cache (they call it KV cache in the infra) was getting stressed, prefix cache pressure then sudden GC-ish behavior. There's also some noisy warmups where long-context requests pushed the sequence length up and the kernel selection started doing the wrong path, leading to extra memory churn.
[01:45] Lena: A few clarifications: our workloads have a heavy tail with some long prompts from our clinician UI, and we do baseline batching which we've tuned to minimize latency. During the test the batch sizes grew unexpectedly because of a burst of long requests.
[02:10] Mei: And adding, we have autoscale on but the node spin-up latency meant the first victims got evicted before capacity came back. So there's a race — eviction + slow warmup + a few large KV entries.
[02:40] Priya: Exactly. Our hypothesis: transient large-key KV cache churn coupled with the batcher forming larger batches that increased peak mem working set. Combined with a kernel switch on some model variants that is heavier on memory.
[03:12] Alex: Is this something that would have been prevented by prefix caching or by pinning model variants?
[03:30] Priya: Pinning helps a lot — if you pin smaller variants for the clinician flows or set an explicit model variant policy (e.g., small-96 for requests under 512 tokens) we avoid the kernel-switch overhead. Prefix caching would help, but the root is the eviction of hot KV entries. If the KV cache had better LRU behavior or larger reserved hot set, that would prevent the cascading evictions.
[04:05] Rajiv: From a security perspective, we also need to validate the KMS rotation and audit logs for the incident. Not because we suspect anything malicious, but auditors will want the timeline correlated with key ops and any exported traces need to be redacted. Can you share what fields you capture?
[04:30] Priya: We'll share sanitized traces. We capture allocation deltas per node, KV cache hit/miss rates, prefix cache sizes, and kernel selector logs. PII is redacted in the export. We can also provide correlation IDs if you want to tie to your internal logs.
[05:05] Samir: Yes, correlation IDs would be useful. Also—how much would a small dedicated pool blunt this? Is it cost-effective?
[05:30] Alex: Short answer — yes it'd reduce noisy neighbor and warmup races because you'd have reserved capacity and fewer cold starts. But there's a cost delta; we'll send a quote. There's also a hybrid: a small dedicated pool + overflow to hosted. That buys you isolation for the hottest flows.
[06:00] Mei: What about fallback oscillation? We actually saw requests flip between a fast fallback and main model because of the canary policy. Some requests got repeated attempts which amplified load.
[06:20] Priya: That's the fallback oscillation problem — when the routing logic sends to fallback and the downstream happens to be slightly faster, the app retries which creates amplification. We can adjust the routing backoff and increase the circuit breaker thresholds in the rollout policy to prevent aggressive retries.
[06:50] Mateo: I'll add that to the runbook — documented thresholds and a 'stop retry' trigger.
[07:15] Lena: For telemetry, what extra metrics should we enable in preprod to catch this earlier?
[07:30] Priya: Add peak working set per process, KVcache tail latency, prefix cache evictions per minute, and kernel-switch counters. Also capture per-request token counts so you can see the long-tail prompts.
[07:55] Samir: Can Redwood run a repro with our exact traffic profile? We can share a sample trace from the window.
[08:10] Priya: Yes — if you share manifests and a replay of the traffic profile we'll run a controlled repro in our lab and try a config where we reserve a hot KV set and tune batcher thresholds.
[08:35] Alex: Quick note on compliance — Rajiv, you'll get the SOC2 info and audit logs. We also maintain SSO/SAML support and can provide role-scoped access for your engineers during the bench.
[09:00] Rajiv: Good. Also any changes that adjust encryption keys—KMS rotations—must be logged for us.
[09:20] Priya: We'll mark those in the exported trace and provide redacted KMS event correlation, not raw keys.
[09:40] Samir: Back to mitigation: what are short-term vs mid-term fixes?
[09:55] Priya: Short-term — increase KV cache reservation, lower batcher max-window and add a conservative fallback backoff. Mid-term — implement a cold-start warmup path for long-context flows and improve kernel selection heuristics to avoid memory heavy paths for certain length distributions. Also a Dedicated pool for the heaviest flows.
[10:30] Mei: So the plan is: we want Redwood to run a focused repro, then we tune preprod, then possibly spin up a small dedicated pool while we roll the kernel change. How long do kernel changes typically take?
[10:50] Priya: Kernel selection heuristics are config-level for many models and can be rolled in a canary within a week, code-level kernel rewrites take longer. For your use-case it's likely config+quantization profile adjustments — a week plus validation.
[11:15] Alex: Any blockers from legal/compliance side for running repro on Redwood preprod with sample traces?
[11:28] Rajiv: We'll need an NDA amendment for data handling, plus the runbook on retention — we have to keep less than 30 days for traces containing PHI.
[11:45] Mateo: We'll coordinate with legal and get an addendum template.
[12:05] Samir: Another question — do you have guardrails for long-running sessions to avoid runaway token growth?
[12:20] Priya: We can implement a token cap per session with a soft warn and hard stop. We also support prefix trimming for clinician flows to keep recent context only.
[12:45] Lena: Could prefix trimming break some clinical flows that rely on long context?
[12:55] Priya: It might. That's why it's a policy you tune per route; we suggest a per-route eval with test prompts.
[13:20] Alex: Alright, I want to switch to concrete deliverables — Priya, what will you run this afternoon?
[13:30] Priya: I'll start the repro with the sample trace once Samir shares the manifest and we'll attach KVcache and kernel logs. Expect a preliminary report in 48–72 hours.
[13:50] Samir: We'll aim to share the manifest by EOD tomorrow.
[14:05] Mateo: I'll draft the runbook and include the circuit-breaker thresholds we discussed.
[14:20] Rajiv: I'll send security constraints and the retention window.
[14:35] Alex: I'll follow up with pricing for a 3-node dedicated pool and overflow settings.
[14:50] Priya: One more technical note — there's an open optimization in our runtime where certain attention kernels allocate transient buffers that can be avoided by using a quantized kernel path; for some model variants switching that path reduces memory overhead 10–15%. We'll test that as part of the repro.
[15:15] Mei: That would be great. It might avoid needing a dedicated pool if we can shave memory out.
[15:35] Alex: We'll also include a recommended monitoring dashboard and alert thresholds.

Recap and explicit next steps (end of call):
[16:00] Mateo: Recap — Redwood to run repro (Priya), customer to share manifest (Samir), runbook update (Mateo), pricing/dedicated rec (Alex), security constraints (Rajiv). Follow-up bench scheduled for 2026-04-13 pending trace review.
[16:25] Samir: Sounds good. Please also include the canary rollback triggers and the 'stop retry' flag for fallbacks.
[16:40] Priya: Noted — we'll add a stop-retry config and canary rollback guard in the runbook.
[16:55] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll be in touch and send the artifact links: runbook draft, repro plan, and sanitized trace template.

Artifacts shared: "repro-plan.md" (link to internal), "sanitized-trace-template.csv" (link), "runbook-draft-v1.pdf" (link to shared drive)

End of transcript.
